missions.title: The Critical Reader Quest
missions.story: During a reading fair, Lian follows a map tied to her grandmother’s memory. Learners investigate story structure, sequence eight events and explain conclusions using evidence.
missions.focus: Literary structure, flashback, eight-event sequencing, inference, figurative meaning and conclusions.

finalChallenge.title: Reader’s Investigation
finalChallenge.description: Reader’s Investigation: arrange all eight story events and choose two pieces of evidence supporting why the book was preserved. Give a short written explanation.

steps.prompt: Reader's Investigation: tap all eight story events in order.
items: The reading fair was announced.
Lian found an old map.
She remembered her grandmother's story.
She asked Guide Mira for help.
They inspected the town-hall plaque.
The plaque directed them to the Word Library.
Lian found the protected book there.
She presented its history at the reading fair.

steps.prompt: Choose TWO pieces of evidence that explain why the book was preserved.
items: It contained stories of how families helped one another during floods.
Lian's grandmother wanted the stories to be remembered.
Lian found the book in the Word Library.
The reading fair was announced.

steps.prompt: In two or three sentences, explain why the book was preserved. Your teacher will read it.

checkpoints.title: Story Garden — The Map and the Memory
checkpoints.reading: During Brightville’s reading fair, Lian found an old map beneath a bench. She remembered her grandmother saying, “Years ago, the town hid a special book to protect its stories.” Lian decided to investigate. She brought the map to Guide Mira, who noticed a symbol shaped like a small leaf.
checkpoints.lesson: Story elements tell us who, where, and what problem moves the plot. A flashback refers to an earlier event. Details can suggest why a character chooses an action.

miniGame.name: Story Map Detective
miniGame.instructions: Tap the present-day event, the remembered past event, and the symbol clue. Match each to its function in the story.

steps.prompt: Story Map Detective: what job does each detail do in the story?
items: Lian found an old map beneath a bench
Lian brought the map to Guide Mira
Her grandmother said the town hid a special book years ago
A symbol shaped like a small leaf
steps.success: You separated the present, the flashback and the clue.

questions.text: Who found the old map during the reading fair?
questions.feedback: Lian discovers the map beneath a bench.

questions.text: Where did Lian find the map?
questions.feedback: The story says it was beneath a bench.

questions.text: Which part of the story refers to an earlier time?
options: Lian remembers her grandmother’s story from years ago
questions.feedback: The remembered statement describes the past.

questions.text: Why does Lian investigate the map?
options: She wants to cancel the fair
She wants to find the book mentioned by her grandmother
She is looking for a lost pet
questions.feedback: The map connects to her grandmother’s story about a hidden book.

questions.text: Which detail is most likely an important clue?
options: The leaf symbol on the map
questions.feedback: Guide Mira specifically identifies the unusual leaf symbol.

checkpoints.title: Truth Hall — Eight Event Trail
checkpoints.reading: Lian’s event notes: 1. The reading fair was announced. 2. Lian found an old map. 3. She remembered her grandmother’s story. 4. She asked Guide Mira for help. 5. They inspected the town-hall plaque. 6. The plaque directed them to the Word Library. 7. Lian found the protected book there. 8. She presented its history at the reading fair.
checkpoints.lesson: A complete sequence puts each event in order. Inferences use clues; figures of speech use expressive language, not always literal descriptions.

miniGame.name: Eight-Card Timeline
miniGame.instructions: Drag all eight event cards into the correct order; highlight the clue that directs Lian toward the library.

steps.prompt: Eight-Card Timeline: tap all eight events in order.
items: The reading fair was announced.
Lian found an old map.
She remembered her grandmother's story.
She asked Guide Mira for help.
They inspected the town-hall plaque.
The plaque directed them to the Word Library.
Lian found the protected book there.
She presented its history at the reading fair.

steps.prompt: Which clue directed Lian toward the library?
items: The reading fair announcement
The old map
The town-hall plaque
Her grandmother's story

questions.text: Which event happened immediately before Lian asked Guide Mira for help?
questions.feedback: Remembering her grandmother’s story is listed directly before visiting Guide Mira.

questions.text: Where did the plaque direct Lian?
questions.feedback: The event notes say the plaque directed them to the library.

questions.text: Which event happened last?
questions.feedback: Sharing the history at the fair completes the sequence.

questions.text: Why was the town-hall plaque important?
options: It gave the next location clue
questions.feedback: The plaque led Lian toward the Word Library.

questions.text: In the sentence “The library was a sea of stories,” what does the phrase suggest?
options: The library was beside the ocean
questions.feedback: The figurative phrase suggests a very large collection of stories.

checkpoints.title: Word Library — Evidence Room
checkpoints.reading: The protected book contained stories of how Brightville families helped one another during earlier floods. Lian realized her grandmother wanted the stories to be remembered, not forgotten. She told the class how the clues led her to the book and why the stories mattered.
checkpoints.lesson: An inference or conclusion must be supported by details. A strong summary includes the important problem, discovery and outcome without adding unrelated information.

miniGame.name: Evidence and Summary Board
miniGame.instructions: Match claims to sentence evidence, then choose the strongest short summary of Lian’s investigation.

steps.prompt: Evidence and Summary Board: which claim does each sentence support?
items: It contained stories of how families helped one another during floods.
Lian realized her grandmother wanted the stories to be remembered.
She told the class how the clues led her to the book.

steps.prompt: Choose the strongest short summary of Lian's investigation.
items: Lian followed clues from an old map to a protected book of flood stories and shared why the stories mattered.
Lian likes maps and goes to the reading fair every year.
Lian's grandmother lives in Brightville and tells many stories.
There is a symbol shaped like a small leaf on a map.

questions.text: What did the protected book contain?
options: Stories of families helping during floods
questions.feedback: It preserved community accounts of mutual help during floods.

questions.text: Why did Lian’s grandmother value the book?
options: She wanted Lian to keep a secret forever
She wanted the community stories remembered
questions.feedback: The passage explains the stories should not be forgotten.

questions.text: What is the best evidence that the book mattered to the community?
options: It recorded families helping during floods
It was stored on a high shelf
questions.feedback: The recorded community experience gives the book significance.

questions.text: Which conclusion follows from the passage?
options: Lian used clues to preserve and share local history
The reading fair had no visitors
questions.feedback: Lian followed evidence and shared what she found at the fair.

questions.text: Which is the best summary?
options: A map was bright and colorful
Lian followed clues to a book of community stories and shared its importance
questions.feedback: This captures the investigation and its meaningful outcome.

missions.title: The Persuasion Investigator
missions.story: A village campaign needs fact-checking. Learners inspect messages, identify persuasive devices, and decide which claims are supported by evidence.
missions.focus: Persuasive texts; author’s purpose; claim and evidence; opinion vs fact; bandwagon, testimonial, and plain-folks techniques.

finalChallenge.title: Campaign Review
finalChallenge.description: Campaign Review: identify three propaganda techniques, choose two reliable pieces of evidence, and produce a respectful two-sentence recommendation for the river campaign.

steps.prompt: Campaign Review: identify the technique used in each message.
items: Everyone in Brightville is joining the clean-up, so you should too!
Mayor Luis says this plan is the best.
I am just a regular neighbor who picks up litter every weekend.

steps.prompt: Choose TWO reliable pieces of evidence for the river campaign.
items: A local audit recorded repeated littering around entrances.
Last month, volunteers collected 25 bags of litter, according to the local clean-up record.
Everyone says the plan is great.
Only foolish people disagree.

steps.prompt: Write a respectful two-sentence recommendation for the river campaign. Your teacher will read it.

checkpoints.title: Story Garden — The Campaign Booth
checkpoints.reading: Poster A: “Keep Brightville River clean! Join the Saturday clean-up.” Poster B: “Everyone is joining, so you should too!” Poster C: “Last month, volunteers collected 25 bags of litter,” according to the local clean-up record.
checkpoints.lesson: Persuasion seeks to influence ideas or actions. A claim needs supporting evidence, while a fact can be checked using reliable records.

miniGame.name: Claim or Evidence?
miniGame.instructions: Sort message cards into Claim, Evidence, and Call to Action.

steps.prompt: Claim or Evidence? Sort each message card.
items: Brightville River needs to be protected.
Litter harms the river.
Last month, volunteers collected 25 bags of litter, according to the local clean-up record.
A local audit recorded repeated littering around the river entrances.
Join the Saturday clean-up.
steps.success: You can tell claims, evidence and calls to action apart.

questions.text: What is the main goal of Poster A?
options: To entertain with a fairy tale
To explain how a river forms
To encourage people to join a clean-up
questions.feedback: The poster calls on residents to participate.

questions.text: Which statement provides a checkable detail?
options: The river is the prettiest place
Volunteers collected 25 bags of litter last month
The clean-up is the best event
questions.feedback: The number can be checked against the cited record.

questions.text: Which sentence is the clearest call to action?
questions.feedback: It directly invites the reader to do something.

questions.text: Which statement expresses an opinion?
options: The clean-up is the best activity of all
questions.feedback: “Best” is a personal judgment rather than a verifiable measurement.

questions.text: What evidence would best support that volunteers collected 25 bags?
questions.feedback: A dated record can verify the stated quantity.

checkpoints.title: Truth Hall — Persuasion Detectives
checkpoints.reading: Message 1: “All your classmates are buying this notebook—join them!” Message 2: “Local teacher Ms. Reyes says this notebook is helpful.” Message 3: “I am an ordinary learner who uses this notebook every day.”
checkpoints.lesson: Bandwagon appeals to what many people supposedly do; testimonial uses a named person’s endorsement; plain folks suggests a speaker is an ordinary person like the audience. Endorsements are not automatically proof.

miniGame.name: Technique Match
miniGame.instructions: Drag each advertising message to Bandwagon, Testimonial or Plain Folks.

steps.prompt: Technique Match: which technique does each message use?
items: All your classmates are buying this notebook. Join them!
Everyone in Grade 6 already uses this bag. Get yours today!
Local teacher Ms. Reyes says this notebook is helpful.
Coach Dana says these shoes are the best.
I am an ordinary learner who uses this notebook every day.

questions.text: Which technique is used in “All your classmates are buying this notebook”?
questions.feedback: It persuades by claiming that many other people are doing it.

questions.text: Which technique uses a teacher’s endorsement?
questions.feedback: A named person recommends the product.

questions.text: Which message uses a plain-folks appeal?
options: I am an ordinary learner who uses this notebook
questions.feedback: The speaker presents themself as an everyday person like the audience.

questions.text: Why should a reader check an endorsement?
options: An endorsement may not be enough evidence of a claim
questions.feedback: An opinion or endorsement is not necessarily independent evidence.

questions.text: Which evidence is strongest for comparing notebook durability?
options: A fair test comparing notebooks under the same conditions
questions.feedback: A consistent comparative test provides evidence about durability.

checkpoints.title: Word Library — Judge the Message
checkpoints.reading: Campaign draft: “Brightville should install more waste bins near the river. A local audit recorded repeated littering around entrances. More clearly labeled bins, along with reminders, may help residents dispose of waste properly.” Another draft says, “Only foolish people disagree with this plan.”
checkpoints.lesson: A credible persuasive message uses a clear claim, relevant reasons, respectful language and checkable evidence; insults are not good arguments.

miniGame.name: Fix the Campaign
miniGame.instructions: Select a claim, pair it with the best supporting evidence, and replace insulting text with respectful language.

steps.prompt: Fix the Campaign, step 1: select the claim.
items: Brightville should install more waste bins near the river.
Only foolish people disagree with this plan.
A local audit recorded repeated littering around entrances.
Waste bins are usually round.

steps.prompt: Step 2: pick the best supporting evidence for that claim.
items: A local audit recorded repeated littering around entrances.
Everyone knows bins are good.
Some people like rivers.
My cousin thinks the plan is nice.

steps.prompt: Step 3: replace “Only foolish people disagree with this plan.” with respectful language.
items: Please read the evidence and share your ideas respectfully.
Anyone who disagrees is silly.
Do not bother disagreeing.
Disagreeing is not allowed.

questions.text: What is the main claim in the campaign draft?
options: More waste bins should be installed near the river
questions.feedback: The draft proposes adding waste bins.

questions.text: Which detail supports the claim?
options: A local audit found littering near entrances
questions.feedback: The audit addresses the problem the proposal is trying to solve.

questions.text: Why is “Only foolish people disagree” a weak argument?
options: It insults people instead of giving evidence
questions.feedback: Personal insults do not support the proposal.

questions.text: Which revision is most respectful?
options: Let us discuss how bins could help keep the river clean
questions.feedback: It invites discussion without insulting anyone.

questions.text: What would improve the campaign most?
options: Cite the audit clearly and explain how bins may help
questions.feedback: Credible evidence and reasoning strengthen the message.

missions.title: The Evidence-Based Communicator
missions.story: Learners help the village plan a school reading campaign using survey findings, a clear message, and effective visuals.
missions.focus: Informational and persuasive organization; survey interpretation; claims and evidence; visual and multimedia communication.

finalChallenge.title: Publish the Reading Corner Plan
finalChallenge.description: Publish the Reading Corner Plan: select a fair survey finding, arrange a short persuasive paragraph, and assemble a two-element flyer (heading + relevant image) with a truthful evidence statement.

steps.prompt: Publish the Reading Corner Plan: select the fair survey finding.
items: Thirty of forty surveyed learners supported a shaded reading space.
Everyone wants the reading space.
Nobody likes the old library.
Forty learners agreed on everything.

steps.prompt: Arrange the persuasive paragraph.
items: Our school should create a shaded reading corner.
Thirty out of forty surveyed learners supported it.
A quiet and comfortable space could help learners enjoy reading.
We can start with available benches and ask the school for feedback.

steps.prompt: Build the flyer: choose the heading.
items: READ TOGETHER! Help us create a shaded reading corner.
EVERYONE MUST READ NOW!!!
Boring flyer

steps.prompt: Choose the relevant image.
items: A book and a shaded bench
A soccer ball
A traffic light

steps.prompt: Choose a truthful evidence statement for the flyer.
items: Survey: 30 of 40 learners supported the idea.
All learners in the world agree.
Nobody disagreed with us.

checkpoints.title: Story Garden — Reading Survey
checkpoints.reading: Forty learners answered a school reading-corner survey. Thirty supported adding a shaded reading space. Twenty-four preferred story-reading sessions after class. The report lists these counts without claiming that everyone agreed.
checkpoints.lesson: A survey asks a clear and fair question. Results should be reported accurately, including who answered and what the numbers show.

miniGame.name: Survey Sorter
miniGame.instructions: Match each statement to Supported, Not Supported or Needs More Evidence; pick a neutral survey question.

steps.prompt: Survey Sorter: does the survey support each statement?
steps.context: Survey: Forty learners answered. Thirty supported adding a shaded reading space. Twenty-four preferred story-reading sessions after class.
items: Thirty of the forty learners supported a shaded reading space.
Twenty-four learners preferred story-reading sessions after class.
All learners agreed to the plan.
Everyone in the school wants a shaded reading space.
Most learners prefer reading outdoors.
steps.success: You read the survey results accurately.

steps.prompt: Which survey question is neutral and fair?
items: Do you support adding a shaded reading space at school: yes, no or not sure?
Don't you agree that a shaded reading space is a great idea?
Wouldn't everyone love a new reading space?
You want the reading space, right?

questions.text: How many learners answered the survey?
questions.feedback: The passage says 40 learners responded.

questions.text: How many supported a shaded reading space?
questions.feedback: Thirty learners supported that idea.

questions.text: Which statement is supported by the survey?
options: Every learner wants a shaded space
Most surveyed learners supported a shaded reading space
questions.feedback: Thirty out of 40 is more than half, but not everyone.

questions.text: Which survey question is least leading?
options: You agree our wonderful reading corner is perfect, right?
Would you use a shaded reading corner at school?
Why do you hate boring books?
questions.feedback: It asks neutrally without suggesting the preferred answer.

questions.text: Which claim would need extra evidence?
options: All students in the school want the same thing
questions.feedback: The sample does not establish what all students in the school want.

checkpoints.title: Truth Hall — Build the Argument
checkpoints.reading: Draft: “Our school should create a shaded reading corner. Thirty out of forty surveyed learners supported it. A quiet and comfortable space could help learners enjoy reading. We can start with available benches and ask the school for feedback.”
checkpoints.lesson: A persuasive paragraph begins with a claim, supports it with relevant evidence, and ends with a practical recommendation or call to action.

miniGame.name: Paragraph Sequencer
miniGame.instructions: Arrange Claim → Evidence → Explanation → Recommendation. Identify an unsupported claim and replace it.

steps.prompt: Paragraph Sequencer: arrange Claim, Evidence, Explanation, Recommendation.
items: Our school should create a shaded reading corner.
Thirty out of forty surveyed learners supported it.
A quiet and comfortable space could help learners enjoy reading.
We can start with available benches and ask the school for feedback.

steps.prompt: Which sentence is an unsupported claim?
items: Every learner in the world loves reading outside.
Thirty out of forty surveyed learners supported it.
We can start with available benches.
Forty learners answered the survey.

steps.prompt: Which sentence replaces it best, using evidence?
items: Thirty out of forty surveyed learners supported a shaded reading space.
Reading outside is the best thing ever.
Nobody likes reading indoors.
Everybody agrees with us.

questions.text: Which sentence states the central claim?
options: Our school should create a shaded reading corner
questions.feedback: It is the recommendation the paragraph seeks to support.

questions.text: Which sentence gives numerical evidence?
options: Thirty out of forty surveyed learners supported it
questions.feedback: The survey result offers checkable support.

questions.text: Which order is clearest for the persuasive paragraph?
questions.feedback: This order introduces an argument and develops it logically.

questions.text: Which statement is too strong for the given evidence?
options: Many surveyed learners support the proposal
Some surveyed learners have different preferences
Every student at school supports the proposal
A reading corner could be considered
questions.feedback: A 40-learner survey does not prove unanimous schoolwide support.

questions.text: What is the best closing sentence?
options: Please consider trying the shaded reading corner and collecting feedback
All other school projects must stop
questions.feedback: It proposes a sensible next step related to the claim.

checkpoints.title: Word Library — Design the Message
checkpoints.reading: Campaign flyer draft: “READ TOGETHER! Help us create a shaded reading corner. Survey: 30 of 40 learners supported the idea. Share your suggestions with the class teacher.” The flyer contains a simple book icon and an illustration of a shaded bench.
checkpoints.lesson: Visuals should strengthen the message, remain readable and fairly represent the evidence. An audience-appropriate design uses clear headings, accurate facts and relevant images.

miniGame.name: Flyer Designer
miniGame.instructions: Choose the correct heading, supportive book/bench icon and evidence statement, then write a short campaign caption.

steps.prompt: Flyer Designer: choose the correct heading.
items: READ TOGETHER! Help us create a shaded reading corner.
EVERYONE MUST READ NOW!!!
Boring flyer
Things and stuff

steps.prompt: Choose the icon that supports the message.
items: A book and a shaded bench
A soccer ball
A traffic light
A birthday balloon

steps.prompt: Choose the truthful evidence statement.
items: Survey: 30 of 40 learners supported the idea.
All learners in the world agree.
Nobody disagreed with us.
Reading makes you rich.

steps.prompt: Write a short caption for your flyer.

questions.text: What is the flyer asking people to support?
questions.feedback: The flyer clearly asks for a reading corner.

questions.text: Which image best fits the flyer?
options: A book beside a shaded bench
questions.feedback: The image directly shows the proposed reading space.

questions.text: Which sentence reports the survey accurately?
options: 30 of 40 surveyed learners supported the idea
questions.feedback: The numbers match the survey data.

questions.text: Who should the flyer address?
options: Students, teachers and the school community
questions.feedback: These groups can consider and respond to a school proposal.

questions.text: Which design choice makes the message clearest?
options: Very tiny text and unrelated icons
A readable heading, brief facts and matching visuals
questions.feedback: The heading, concise facts and relevant images reinforce each other.
